items.title: No hostels, no enforcement: Decoding Delhi’s student housing crisis
items.summary: This country keeps failing its students, whether they are in government schools far from the city or in expensive PGs in the capital. Seven people have died, out of the 12 rescued so far, after a five-storey building collapsed in Delhi's Satya Niketan on Sunday. Among the dead are Arpit, a second-year B.Com student at Atma Ram Sanatan Dharma (ARSD) College; Abhishek Kumar, a student of Motilal Nehru College; and 18-year-old Akshat from Madhya Pradesh’s Katni. Akshat’s friend said he had returned to Delhi only two days ago, after Raksha Bandhan, and that he wanted to become an IAS officer. Others are still to be identified and rescued. Local students said that since it was a Sunday, they expected anywhere between 25 and 40 students to still be trapped. The building was built in the late 1990s on a 55-square-yard plot and was gradually converted into a paying guest (PG) accommodation. Locals said construction work on old shops on the ground floor was underway before the collapse. items.title: Why courts extend arbitration deadlines, not replace arbitrators? Justice Bharati Dangre explains
items.summary: Replacing an arbitrator after years of hearings can wipe out substantial time, money and effort already spent in the proceedings, Bombay High Court judge Justice Bharati Dangre said while explaining why courts often grant extensions under Section 29A of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. " If I turn it down today and appoint a new arbitrator, what happens to all that effort, all that resources which have gone for all these years? " Justice Dangre said. She added that courts may therefore grant a short extension if it ultimately serves the interests of justice. Justice Dangre was speaking during a fireside chat with Senior Advocate Vikram Nankani at India ADR Week 2026 in Mumbai, organised by the Mumbai Centre for International Arbitration (MCIA). During the discussion, Nankani asked about her transition from Nagpur to Mumbai and her experience of handling commercial matters. Justice Dangre said that her earlier practice, largely involving civil and criminal matters for the government, had given her little exposure to arbitration.
